summary: The messengers of Beis Din prepared the barley for the omer before Yom Tov, and many people came to watch. After dark on the first night of Pesach, the reaper asked the crowd again and again if it was time and if he should cut. This was to show the Baysusim, who said the omer may not be cut right after Yom Tov, that they were wrong.

summary: Once the omer was brought, the new grain became allowed, and the market in Yerushalayim filled with flour and toasted grain. After the Churban, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai made a rule that the new grain is forbidden the whole day of the waving. People far away could eat from midday, because they knew Beis Din would not be lazy.

summary: Before the omer, grain may be cut to save young trees, to make room for a house of mourning, or so learning in the beis midrash is not stopped, but it must not be tied into bundles. The best way is to cut the omer from standing, fresh grain at night, but it is kosher otherwise, and cutting it is allowed on Shabbos.

chunks.st: and due to the need to create room for students to study, as failure to do so would lead to dereliction of Torah study in the study hall.
